en.statement: GitLab uses the order of YAML keywords in `.gitlab-ci.yml` to schedule jobs.
en.explanation: YAML mapping key order does not schedule jobs; configuration keywords define the execution order.

en.statement: GitLab appends `default:before_script` commands to a job's own `before_script` commands.
en.explanation: A job's own `before_script` replaces the corresponding default value instead of combining with it.

en.statement: GitLab passes global `default` keywords from a parent pipeline into its child pipeline.
en.explanation: Global job defaults stay within their pipeline. A downstream pipeline uses its own configuration defaults.

en.statement: A job can use `inherit:variables` to select the top-level variables it receives.
en.explanation: A list under `inherit:variables` preserves the named defaults and excludes the other top-level variables.

en.statement: Omitting `stages` gives a pipeline `.pre`, `build`, `test`, `deploy` and `.post`.
en.explanation: When top-level `stages` is omitted, GitLab supplies `.pre`, `build`, `test`, `deploy` and `.post` in that order.

en.statement: A job that omits `stage` joins the first stage listed in the pipeline's `stages` array.
en.explanation: GitLab assigns a job that omits `stage` to `test`, regardless of which stage appears first.

en.statement: Jobs assigned to the same stage can execute concurrently when runners are available.
en.explanation: Jobs in one stage share an execution level, so available runners can execute them concurrently.

en.statement: By default, GitLab cancels running jobs in a stage when another job in that stage fails.
en.explanation: Running jobs in the current stage continue after a peer fails under the default failure behavior.

en.statement: A pipeline containing just `.pre` and `.post` jobs runs those jobs in their stage order.
en.explanation: A pipeline needs at least one job in a stage other than `.pre` or `.post` to run.

en.statement: A job name beginning with a dot makes its configuration available as a hidden template.
en.explanation: GitLab skips execution of jobs whose names start with a dot while retaining their configuration for reuse.

en.statement: CI Lint validates CI/CD configuration supplied through `include` in `.gitlab-ci.yml`.
en.explanation: CI Lint checks included configuration as part of its syntax validation.

en.statement: GitLab Runner runs `before_script` and `script` in one shell for each job.
en.explanation: The runner combines these sections, so shell state from `before_script` remains available in `script`.

en.statement: A job's `after_script` commands can read variables that its `script` commands export.
en.explanation: GitLab Runner starts `after_script` in a separate shell; variables exported in `script` do not carry over.

en.statement: Since GitLab 17.0, canceling a job during `script` starts its configured `after_script`.
en.explanation: Normal cancellation runs the cleanup section before the job reaches its final canceled state.

en.statement: By default, a job whose `script` succeeded still passes when its `after_script` fails.
en.explanation: GitLab Runner ignores after_script errors by default, so the job keeps the result of its script. Setting the AFTER_SCRIPT_IGNORE_ERRORS variable to false makes such an error fail the job.

en.statement: GitLab runs a job's `after_script` after a failure classified as `script_failure`.
en.explanation: After a job failure, GitLab runs `after_script` for `script_failure`, rather than other failure types.

en.statement: A failed job with `allow_failure: true` triggers later jobs that use `when: on_failure`.
en.explanation: Allowed failures count as successful when GitLab decides whether later `on_failure` jobs should run.

en.statement: `retry:when` and `retry:exit_codes` combine as an AND condition for automatic job retries.
en.explanation: GitLab retries when either the configured failure type or a listed exit code matches, within the `retry:max` budget.

en.statement: A job's `timeout` value takes precedence over a shorter maximum timeout set on its runner.
en.explanation: The runner's maximum job timeout caps execution even when the job requests a longer timeout.

en.statement: In conservative mode, a started `script` job with `interruptible: false` blocks new-commit auto-cancel.
en.explanation: In conservative mode, a started script job with `interruptible: false` keeps its pipeline running when a newer pipeline starts for the same ref.

en.statement: `workflow:auto_cancel:on_job_failure: all` confines cancellation to the failing job's stage.
en.explanation: `workflow:auto_cancel:on_job_failure: all` cancels the pipeline and its running jobs across stages.

en.statement: `needs` lets a test job start while unrelated build jobs are still running.
en.explanation: GitLab schedules the consumer after its listed producers finish instead of waiting for their whole stage.

source.title: Make jobs start earlier with needs

en.statement: `needs: []` makes GitLab wait for the previous stage before starting a job.
en.explanation: An empty `needs` list schedules the job as soon as GitLab creates the pipeline.

source.title: Make jobs start earlier with needs

en.statement: In one stage, a job that lists another job of the same stage in `needs` waits for that job to finish before it starts.
en.explanation: A job's needs can name a job in its own stage. The job then waits for that job to finish, so jobs of one stage can run in sequence.

en.statement: `needs` on a parallel job lets its consumer start once any one of its instances succeeds.
en.explanation: A plain dependency on a parallel job waits for every instance of that producer.

en.statement: A job with `needs` downloads artifacts from each completed job in earlier stages.
en.explanation: A job using `needs` restricts artifact downloads to the producers named in its dependency list.

en.statement: A `needs` entry with `artifacts: false` keeps the dependency while skipping its artifacts.
en.explanation: A `needs` entry keeps its scheduling dependency when `artifacts: false` disables the producer's artifact download.

en.statement: GitLab can create a pipeline when `rules` exclude a job named in a required `needs` entry.
en.explanation: A missing required producer prevents pipeline creation. Mark a potentially absent producer with `needs:optional`.

source.title: Make jobs start earlier with needs

en.statement: A matching `rules:needs` adds its jobs to the job-level `needs` list.
en.explanation: `rules:needs` in a matching rule replaces the job's entire `needs` configuration.

en.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, `needs:project` waits for an active upstream pipeline to finish.
en.explanation: `needs:project` fetches the specified job's latest successful artifacts for that ref while another pipeline may run.

en.statement: `needs:pipeline` copies the latest pipeline status from another project's default branch.
en.explanation: GitLab mirrors the upstream default-branch pipeline's status onto the configured job.

en.statement: GitLab lets later matching job rules change attributes set by an earlier matching rule.
en.explanation: GitLab stops evaluating a job's `rules` at the first match and uses that rule's attributes.

source.title: Specify when jobs run with rules

en.statement: A rule containing `if`, `changes` and `exists` matches when each condition succeeds.
en.explanation: GitLab combines the conditions within one rule with AND logic.

source.title: Specify when jobs run with rules

en.statement: `rules:when: manual` gives a job `allow_failure: true` by default.
en.explanation: A manual job defined inside `rules` defaults to `allow_failure: false`.

en.statement: A matched rule's `when` value overrides the job-level `when` value for that job.
en.explanation: GitLab applies the matching rule's scheduling choice when both locations specify `when`.

en.statement: `rules:if` supports RE2 syntax when GitLab compares a variable to a regular expression.
en.explanation: GitLab evaluates regular expression comparisons using RE2 syntax.

source.title: Specify when jobs run with rules

en.statement: `rules:if` matches a slash-delimited variable on the right of `=~` as literal text.
en.explanation: GitLab treats a valid slash-delimited pattern held in the right-hand variable as a regular expression.

source.title: Specify when jobs run with rules

en.statement: `rules:changes` in a scheduled pipeline checks differences from the previous commit by default.
en.explanation: Scheduled pipelines lack a push event, so `rules:changes` is true unless `compare_to` defines a comparison.

en.statement: `rules:changes` uses the target branch as its comparison base in merge request pipelines.
en.explanation: GitLab compares the merge request's listed file paths against its target branch.

en.statement: Job-level `rules:exists` searches the pipeline's own project and ref by default.
en.explanation: GitLab checks the listed paths in that project and ref unless the rule specifies another project.

en.statement: `workflow:rules` controls whether GitLab creates a pipeline for a particular triggering event.
en.explanation: GitLab applies workflow rules before selecting the jobs that would belong to the pipeline.

en.statement: `workflow:rules` supports `when: manual` for a user to start the pipeline.
en.explanation: GitLab accepts `always` and `never` as the `when` values in `workflow:rules`. Manual scheduling applies to jobs.

en.statement: A matching `workflow:rules:variables` value overrides the same top-level YAML variable.
en.explanation: GitLab uses the matching workflow rule's value instead of the top-level YAML default for that name.

en.statement: `workflow:name` can combine fixed text with CI/CD variable values.
en.explanation: GitLab expands variable references when assigning the configured pipeline name.

en.statement: GitLab sets `CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE` to `api` for a pipeline started with New pipeline in the project UI.
en.explanation: A pipeline started with New pipeline in the project UI has `CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE` set to `web`.

source.title: Specify when jobs run with rules

en.statement: `CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` contains the source branch name in merge request pipelines.
en.explanation: `CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` is available in branch pipelines but unavailable in merge request pipelines.

en.statement: `workflow:rules` can suppress branch pipelines when `CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS` has a value.
en.explanation: GitLab's workflow example rejects a branch pipeline when that branch has an open merge request, avoiding duplicate pipelines.

en.statement: GitLab marks an empty push pipeline created by a `[ci skip]` commit message as successful.
en.explanation: GitLab still creates an empty pipeline for the skipped push and gives it the Skipped status.

en.statement: The `ci.skip` push option can skip merge request pipelines associated with the push.
en.explanation: The `ci.skip` push option skips push pipelines and leaves associated merge request pipelines eligible to run.

en.statement: GitLab uses the schedule owner's permissions for automatic scheduled pipeline runs.
en.explanation: The schedule owner supplies the access level used for automatic scheduled runs.

en.statement: A job's YAML variable overrides a top-level variable with the same name.
en.explanation: A job-level YAML value customizes that job. Other jobs keep the same-named top-level default unless they override it too.

en.statement: A job's `variables: {}` preserves variables defined at the top level.
en.explanation: An empty job variables map suppresses top-level YAML variable defaults.

en.statement: A project's Developer role can edit CI/CD variables in the project's settings.
en.explanation: Changing project CI/CD variables requires the Maintainer role or higher.

en.statement: When a parent group and its subgroup both define `DEPLOY_ENV`, jobs in the subgroup's projects get the subgroup's value.
en.explanation: An inherited group variable comes from the nearest subgroup that defines its name, rather than a more distant ancestor.

en.statement: On GitLab Self-Managed, the group Owner role grants permission to create instance CI/CD variables.
en.explanation: Creating instance CI/CD variables requires administrator access on GitLab Self-Managed.

en.statement: GitLab gives project variables higher precedence than same-named job-level YAML variables.
en.explanation: A value in project CI/CD settings takes priority over a job's YAML value, even when the YAML declares it inside that job.

en.statement: A manual job uses the user's job variables ahead of same-named pipeline variables.
en.explanation: Variables entered when starting a manual job outrank existing pipeline variables, so the entered value wins a name collision.

en.statement: Multi-project triggers passing variables use the upstream Minimum role to use pipeline variables setting.
en.explanation: For a multi-project trigger that passes variables, GitLab checks the user's downstream role against the downstream project's Minimum role to use pipeline variables setting.

en.statement: A job receives the stored contents as the environment value of a file type CI/CD variable.
en.explanation: For a file type CI/CD variable, GitLab sets the environment value to the path of a temporary file containing the stored value.

en.statement: Since GitLab 18.6, GitLab leaves Expand variable reference off for new UI variables by default.
en.explanation: Values such as `$OTHER_VAR` stay literal until the creator enables Expand variable reference.

en.statement: Since GitLab 18.1, a project setting lets eligible merge request pipelines read protected variables.
en.explanation: A merge request pipeline gets protected variables when the project allows access, both branches are protected in the same project, and its triggering user can push or merge to the target branch.

en.statement: Since GitLab 18.3, GitLab selects Masked by default for new CI/CD variables created in the UI.
en.explanation: GitLab starts a new UI variable with Masked visibility; its creator can select a different visibility.

en.statement: A Maintainer can block malicious job scripts from reading a variable by choosing Masked visibility.
en.explanation: Masking redacts matching values in logs. A job's script still has access to the variable's value.

en.statement: A Maintainer can switch an existing variable's visibility to Masked and hidden.
en.explanation: A creator chooses Masked and hidden when adding a variable. GitLab prevents changing an existing variable to hidden.

en.statement: A pipeline running in a fork reads the parent project's CI/CD variables by default.
en.explanation: A pipeline running in a fork uses the fork's variables rather than the parent project's variables.

en.statement: GitLab keeps CI_JOB_TOKEN valid until the pipeline finishes.
en.explanation: GitLab revokes CI_JOB_TOKEN when its job finishes, even if other jobs keep the pipeline running.

en.statement: CI_JOB_TOKEN uses the access level of the user who starts the job.
en.explanation: A job token receives its triggering user's access level for the GitLab resources available to job tokens.

en.statement: Since GitLab 19.0, GitLab issues CI/CD job tokens in JWT format by default.
en.explanation: JWT is the default job-token format. A top-level group can select the legacy format during GitLab 19.x.

en.statement: GitLab grants extra project permissions to members of projects added to its CI/CD job token allowlist.
en.explanation: Adding a project to the CI/CD job token allowlist permits token access subject to the user's existing permissions in the target project.

en.statement: GitLab starts a pipeline by default for a successful repository push authenticated with CI_JOB_TOKEN.
en.explanation: A successful Git push using CI_JOB_TOKEN creates no CI/CD pipeline in the target project.

en.statement: A job can set different `aud` values for its named `id_tokens`.
en.explanation: Each named ID token has its configured audience, so one job can request tokens for different services.

source.title: OpenID Connect (OIDC) Authentication Using ID Tokens

en.statement: The Maintainer role grants a project member permission to create a project runner.
en.explanation: GitLab requires the Maintainer role or higher when a project member creates a project runner.

en.statement: GitLab returns a runner authentication token when a user creates a runner for registration.
en.explanation: Create the runner first, then register GitLab Runner with the returned runner authentication token.

source.title: Migrating to the new runner registration workflow

en.statement: A runner matches a tagged job when it shares at least one tag with the job.
en.explanation: A runner needs every tag the job lists. Sharing just one tag does not satisfy a job's complete tag list.

en.statement: Protected runners can execute jobs in pipelines for protected tags.
en.explanation: A protected tag satisfies a protected runner's ref restriction; the job still has to meet that runner's other selection criteria.

en.statement: Locking a project runner makes GitLab remove its existing assignments to other projects.
en.explanation: Locking a project runner retains its current project assignments and prevents enabling it in additional projects.

en.statement: Instance runners use a first in, first out queue to select jobs across projects.
en.explanation: Instance runners use a fair usage queue, favoring projects with fewer jobs already running.

en.statement: The Kubernetes executor runs the jobs of one pipeline stage in the same Pod.
en.explanation: GitLab Runner asks Kubernetes to create a fresh Pod for each CI/CD job.

en.statement: `image:docker` configures image options for jobs running with the Kubernetes executor.
en.explanation: GitLab supports image:docker options with both the Docker and Kubernetes executors.

en.statement: GitLab Runner applies its `concurrent` limit separately to each runner configuration.
en.explanation: The concurrent setting caps the combined running jobs across the runner configurations managed by one process.

en.statement: GitLab recommends keeping GitLab Runner's major.minor version aligned with GitLab's.
en.explanation: Matching major.minor versions helps ensure features that need a matching GitLab Runner version work properly.

en.statement: GitLab.com hosted Linux runners require job authors to declare a runner tag.
en.explanation: GitLab.com hosted Linux runners accept untagged jobs; a job tag is optional for the default hosted routing.

en.statement: Jobs in different projects can share one cache by choosing the same `cache:key`.
en.explanation: GitLab scopes caches to a project. Matching cache keys do not make one project's cache available to another.

en.statement: GitLab separates caches for protected and non-protected branches by default.
en.explanation: Separate cache keys form a security boundary. A project can change this default behavior.

en.statement: `cache:key:files` derives the cache key from the contents of the files a job lists.
en.explanation: GitLab bases this key on listed file contents, so a changed dependency lockfile selects a new cache.

en.statement: A job can continue when GitLab Runner misses both the requested cache and its fallback caches.
en.explanation: A cache miss leaves the job running with no restored cache. The script may need to recreate the missing files.

en.statement: GitLab Runner restores a job's cache before it downloads the job's artifacts.
en.explanation: Artifact extraction happens after cache restoration, so an artifact can replace a cached file at the same path.

en.statement: GitLab Runner uploads a generated `artifacts:reports` file even when the job's script fails.
en.explanation: Report artifacts upload for both successful and failed jobs, so GitLab can retain reports from a failed test run.

en.statement: Jobs in later stages download artifacts from jobs in previous pipeline stages by default.
en.explanation: GitLab places the earlier jobs' artifacts in the consuming job's working directory.

en.statement: A job's `dependencies` list supports downloading artifacts from another job in the same stage.
en.explanation: The dependencies list accepts jobs from earlier stages. Its stage restriction excludes jobs in the consuming job's own stage.

en.statement: GitLab Runner uploads `artifacts:paths` after a job times out when `artifacts:when` is `always`.
en.explanation: Setting artifacts:when to always still skips ordinary artifact uploads for jobs that time out.

en.statement: By default, GitLab deletes a branch's newest successful pipeline artifacts once their `artifacts:expire_in` time passes.
en.explanation: By default, GitLab keeps the artifacts of each ref's latest pipeline and of its most recent successful pipeline, and expire_in does not apply to them. A project can turn this off.

en.statement: GitLab creates a missing environment when a deployment job declares it with `environment`.
en.explanation: An environment entry in a deployment job creates the named environment if the project does not have it yet.

en.statement: A deployment job can use a variable exported in `script` to build its `environment:name` value.
en.explanation: GitLab expands environment:name before the job script runs, so script-created variables are unavailable for that name.

en.statement: A deployment job puts the shell commands that clean up its environment directly in `environment:on_stop`.
en.explanation: The on_stop value names a separate stop job; that job's script performs the cleanup.

en.statement: Under the default stopping behavior, GitLab stops an environment when its associated branch is deleted.
en.explanation: GitLab's default stopping behavior links an environment's lifetime to its associated branch.

en.statement: Each deployment resets the environment's expiry period specified by `environment:auto_stop_in`.
en.explanation: A new deployment starts the configured lifetime again, extending the environment's scheduled stop time.

en.statement: GitLab creates a deployment record for an environment when a job uses `environment:action: prepare`.
en.explanation: The prepare environment action accesses the environment for preparation and bypasses deployment creation.

en.statement: GitLab marks a pipeline as failed while it waits for a blocking manual deployment job.
en.explanation: A pipeline waiting for a blocking manual job has blocked status. Running the job lets the pipeline continue.

en.statement: GitLab starts the `start_in` timer of a delayed job in the deploy stage while the build and test stages still run.
en.explanation: A delayed job's timer starts only after the previous stage completes successfully, so the start_in wait adds to the time the earlier stages take.

en.statement: GitLab runs the `resource_group: production` jobs of two pipelines on different branches of one project one at a time.
en.explanation: A resource group makes a job mutually exclusive across the project's pipelines, whatever their branch, so a job waits while another job of that group runs.

en.statement: Prevent outdated deployment jobs determines deployment job age from the commit timestamp.
en.explanation: GitLab determines deployment job age from the job's start time rather than the commit time.

en.statement: Rules on an `include:` entry, such as an `include:component`, count as the rules that merge request pipelines need.
en.explanation: Rules defined in include:, for example with include:component, do not count. Merge request pipelines need job rules or workflow:rules that match CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event".

en.statement: A merge request pipeline tests the source branch's contents alone.
en.explanation: GitLab uses the source branch for a merge request pipeline and ignores the target branch's content.

en.statement: GitLab runs a fork's merge request pipeline in the parent project by default.
en.explanation: GitLab normally creates and runs a fork's merge request pipeline in the fork project.

en.statement: For a fork merge request pipeline run in the parent project, GitLab reads the parent's branch configuration.
en.explanation: A fork's merge request pipeline run in the parent project uses the CI/CD configuration from the fork's branch.

en.statement: GitLab asks users to accept a warning before starting a fork merge request pipeline in the parent project's UI.
en.explanation: The UI requires the parent project member to accept a warning before starting a pipeline for a fork's merge request.

en.statement: With merged results pipelines in GitLab Premium and Ultimate, branch conflicts make GitLab run a merge request pipeline.
en.explanation: Conflicting source and target changes prevent a temporary merged result, so GitLab runs a standard merge request pipeline instead.

en.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, merge trains support projects with merged results pipelines turned off.
en.explanation: GitLab requires merged results pipelines to be enabled before a project uses merge trains.

en.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, a merge train pipeline includes every preceding merge request's changes in that train.
en.explanation: GitLab combines a queued merge request's changes with those ahead of it to test compatibility with the earlier changes.

en.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, merge train pipelines use sequential execution by default.
en.explanation: GitLab runs merge train pipelines in parallel when capacity is available.

en.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, GitLab keeps a merge request on its train after that request's train pipeline fails.
en.explanation: GitLab removes a merge request from its train when that merge request's train pipeline fails.

en.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, `rules:changes:compare_to` can match target-branch changes in merged results pipelines.
en.explanation: The temporary merged commit includes target-branch changes. These can make rules:changes:compare_to match more than the merge request's own changes.

en.statement: A trigger job can reserve a runner slot while GitLab creates its downstream pipeline.
en.explanation: GitLab creates downstream pipelines itself; trigger jobs use no runner.

en.statement: A trigger job succeeds by default as soon as GitLab creates its downstream pipeline.
en.explanation: The default trigger status records successful pipeline creation rather than the result of the downstream jobs.

en.statement: A child pipeline runs against the same commit SHA as the parent pipeline that creates it.
en.explanation: A child pipeline uses the parent's project, ref and commit, so a later branch update does not change its checkout.

en.statement: GitLab can auto-cancel interruptible child pipelines when a new commit gets a pipeline on the same ref.
en.explanation: Child pipelines participate in redundant-pipeline auto-cancellation when their jobs are configured to permit interruption.

en.statement: A multi-project trigger uses the upstream branch name as its downstream branch by default.
en.explanation: GitLab selects the downstream project's default branch unless the trigger job sets trigger:branch.

en.statement: The user triggering a multi-project pipeline requires permission to run pipelines in the downstream project.
en.explanation: GitLab checks the initiating user's access to the downstream project before creating that project's pipeline.

en.statement: A child of a merge request pipeline has `CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE` set to `merge_request_event`.
en.explanation: GitLab sets CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE to parent_pipeline in a child pipeline, including one whose parent is a merge request pipeline.

en.statement: A trigger job can read its child pipeline configuration from a YAML file saved as a job artifact.
en.explanation: trigger:include identifies the generated YAML with artifact and its producing job with job.

en.statement: Trigger jobs forward pipeline variables to their downstream pipelines by default.
en.explanation: By default, trigger jobs keep pipeline variables upstream. Set pipeline_variables: true under trigger:forward to pass them.

en.statement: The docs suggest a full 40-character SHA as the `include:project` ref for the most stable result.
en.explanation: A short SHA can be ambiguous, while the full SHA ensures GitLab reads the intended commit. A fully qualified ref such as refs/tags/<tag> is the other suggested option.

en.statement: An `include` placed at the bottom of `.gitlab-ci.yml` lets included keys override the file's own keys.
en.explanation: GitLab evaluates included files first wherever the include keyword appears, so values in .gitlab-ci.yml take precedence over included ones.

en.statement: A job in `.gitlab-ci.yml` that reuses an included job's name discards that included job's other keys.
en.explanation: GitLab merges same-named jobs from included files and .gitlab-ci.yml, so keys the local job leaves unset keep their included values.

source.title: Use CI/CD configuration from other files

en.statement: Retrying a single job after an included file changes makes GitLab fetch that included file again.
en.explanation: A retried job uses the configuration GitLab fetched when it created the pipeline. A new pipeline fetches the included files again and picks up changes.

en.statement: A nested `include:local` in a file from another project resolves its path in that other project.
en.explanation: GitLab evaluates include based on the location of the file that contains it, not the project running the pipeline.

en.statement: For a private `include:project` source, the pipeline user needs at least the Reporter role in that project.
en.explanation: With a lower role, GitLab shows a not found or access denied error. Internal projects accept any authenticated non-external user and public projects need no membership.

en.statement: `include:remote` sends an access token header so GitLab can fetch a YAML file from a private URL.
en.explanation: include:remote fetches the URL with a plain HTTP or HTTPS GET and supports no authentication. For a file in a private project on the same instance, use include:project.

en.statement: With `include:integrity`, GitLab fails the pipeline when the remote file's SHA256 hash differs from the given one.
en.explanation: include:integrity takes a Base64-encoded SHA256 hash of an include:remote file. On a mismatch GitLab does not process the file, which guards against changed remote content.

en.statement: With `extends`, a job's own `script` array replaces the template's `script` instead of adding to it.
en.explanation: extends deep-merges hashes such as variables but replaces arrays such as script and tags with the value from the last member.

en.statement: A job using `extends` still inherits the template's `variables` when it sets its own `variables: null`.
en.explanation: Assigning null to a key in a job that uses extends excludes that key from the extended content, so the job keeps none of the template's variables.

en.statement: A YAML alias in `.gitlab-ci.yml` can point to an anchor defined in a file added with `include`.
en.explanation: YAML anchors are valid in the file that defines them. To reuse configuration from another file, use extends or !reference tags.

en.statement: A job can build its `rules` array from several `!reference` tags that point at rule lists elsewhere.
en.explanation: Each tag inserts the rule list it points at, and GitLab combines the lists into one rules array, so shared rule sets can be mixed per job.

en.statement: A component can be a `templates/<name>/` directory, whose `template.yml` is the one file other projects use.
en.explanation: Other files in that directory, such as tests or a Dockerfile, are not released with the component. A single templates/<name>.yml file is the alternative layout.

en.statement: Each component in a component project gets its own version, independent of the project's other components.
en.explanation: All components in a component project are versioned together. A component that needs different versioning belongs in a dedicated component project.

en.statement: On GitLab Self-Managed, `include:component` can load a component straight from GitLab.com.
en.explanation: include:component references components on the same GitLab instance as the project. To use a GitLab.com component on GitLab Self-Managed, mirror its project there (Premium and Ultimate).

en.statement: `~latest` in `include:component` picks a pre-release like `2.0.0-rc` when it is the newest published version.
en.explanation: ~latest and partial versions skip pre-releases, which GitLab does not treat as production-ready. To use one, reference its full version, such as 2.0.0-rc.

en.statement: Publishing a component version to the CI/CD Catalog requires a CI/CD job that uses the `release` keyword.
en.explanation: The catalog accepts releases created by the release keyword in a job, not through the Releases API, typically in a pipeline for a semantic version tag.

en.statement: `spec:inputs` belongs in a header that a `---` line separates from the rest of the configuration file.
en.explanation: spec is a header keyword declared at the top of the file. When the file also defines jobs, the --- YAML document separator ends the header.

en.statement: An input in `spec:inputs` that omits `default` is optional for configurations that include the file.
en.explanation: Inputs are mandatory unless spec:inputs:default sets a default value, so each include of the file must set them under include:inputs.

en.statement: An input that omits `spec:inputs:type` accepts any YAML value, including arrays and booleans.
en.explanation: Inputs expect strings unless spec:inputs:type sets array, number or boolean.

en.statement: Since GitLab 19.0, `options` can restrict which values an `array` type input accepts.
en.explanation: The pipeline fails to start if any item of the array input is missing from the options list. A manual run shows the options as a multi-select list.
